blocks.text: From a Detectable Response to a Usable Test

blocks.body:
Our initial experimental question was whether engineered yeast could sense candidate ascaroside signals and convert that response into a visible color. Surveys, expert interviews, university exchanges, and farm visits expanded this into more specific questions: when should testing take place, how might soil alter the signal, is a sample representative, and how would a user interpret the result?

Our Human Practices and laboratory research therefore inform each other. Wet-lab and dry-lab insights help frame survey and interview questions; responses and professional advice add evidence for discussions about targets, models, controls, and conditions of use. The following sections trace these connections. Full accounts of the activities appear on the Investigation page.

blocks.text: A Two-Way Link Between the Questionnaire and Research

blocks.body: Our questionnaire on agricultural nematodes and detection needs was developed alongside the research. Drawing on existing wet-lab and dry-lab findings and the proposed application, we asked about awareness of underground disease, expectations of testing, and interpretation of results. Team networks and teaching partnerships helped extend its reach.

This process helped us translate technical ideas into questions that respondents could answer. While our project investigates nematode-associated chemical signals, potential users ask why testing is needed and what a result can tell them. We therefore translated experimental terminology into concrete situations and organized responses as information about needs for the wet-lab and dry-lab teams.

Questionnaire responses help us understand what information people need, how they interpret a test result, and which features they value in a testing tool. Together with expert advice and university exchanges, these findings inform discussions of research priorities and potential use within our wet-lab and dry-lab work.

We collected 369 questionnaire submissions between April 14 and August 6, 2026. Self-reported locations spanned 23 provincial-level regions and 56 distinct city or district entries. Team channels and teaching partnerships helped bring agricultural nematodes into wider public discussion.

Of the 369 respondents, 197 (53.4%) had either never heard of plant-parasitic nematodes or had heard the term without knowing the details. This helped define our educational starting point: explain what nematodes are and why their damage can be difficult to recognize before introducing the detection concept.

When asked to select up to three features of an ideal testing tool, 261 respondents chose ease of use (70.7%), 208 chose accuracy and reliability (56.4%), and 199 chose affordability (53.9%). These responses made usability, trustworthy results, and accessible cost priorities in our discussions of potential use. Percentages use all 369 responses to this multiple-choice question as the denominator.

The questionnaire mainly reached students and people working in research or education, with many submissions from Shandong and Tianjin. We use it to understand the awareness and expectations of the people reached, alongside expert advice and growers’ accounts of specific needs.

blocks.text: Question One  How Early Is Early Enough

blocks.body: Qian Liu directed our discussion toward decisions made before planting. For nematode diseases that require preventive management, detection before obvious above-ground symptoms may still be too late to guide action. Testing needs to be considered alongside the intended crop, soil conditions, and subsequent management. Yurong Yao’s account of hidden root damage and practical barriers to testing added agricultural context to this discussion.

This prompted us to define “early” more precisely: when should a sample be collected, which decision should the result inform, and how long can the user wait? These discussions help our wet-lab and dry-lab teams relate detection goals to potential use.

Pre-planting screening consequently became an important setting for evaluating potential value. The contribution of HP was to clarify the timing and decision that testing should serve, rather than judging usefulness by readout speed alone.

blocks.text: Question Two  How Does Soil Affect Signals and Color

blocks.body: Zhihao Pang noted that differences in soil background color could affect visual interpretation. He also raised a question for the model: if ascr#3 and ascr#18 degrade at different rates in soil, would their measured relative abundance still represent the original signal composition? This prompted us to consider environmental processes when interpreting ratios in soil.

This feedback prompted us to consider the soil environment when discussing signal interpretation. Signal stability, background interference, and differences between laboratory and field conditions are shared considerations for the wet-lab and dry-lab teams.

Qian Liu also suggested progressing from simpler sample conditions to real field samples. Her advice informed discussions of validation priorities and helped us understand the relationship between a laboratory response and potential field use.

blocks.text: Question Three  What Makes a Sample Meaningful and a Test Usable

blocks.body: Yurong Yao described uneven nematode distribution within fields, differences between greenhouses, and the importance of sample transport, storage, separate handling, and disposal. Qian Liu also emphasized that representativeness, losses during separation and extraction, and matrix inhibition affect interpretation. A result from one sample cannot automatically describe an entire field.

Our soil collection and sampling guidance therefore need to retain sample identifiers, crop, location, date, and treatment history. These records allow later experiments to compare sample conditions and help the dry-lab team distinguish information suitable for analysis from differences that need separate consideration.

For end users, Yao emphasized affordability and straightforward interpretation, while Pang recommended minimizing operational steps. Together, their advice extended portability from a device feature to the whole workflow: sampling, preparation, reaction, interpretation, and post-test handling all need to be practical.

blocks.text: Lessons for Our Research and Other Teams

blocks.body:
### Inputs to Our Wet-Lab and Dry-Lab Work {#hp-source-103}

HP provides our wet-lab and dry-lab teams with information about needs, professional perspectives, and application settings. The questionnaire describes public understanding and expectations of a test; experts add perspectives on timing, samples, and usability; university exchanges offer comparisons of experimental approaches; and farm visits provide local agricultural context. Together, these inputs support discussions of research direction and potential value.

### Practices Other Teams Can Adapt {#hp-source-105}

First, retain the link between an experimental question, a survey question, the responses, and the resulting research discussion. Other teams can begin with their own technical assumptions when designing a questionnaire, rather than distributing a general awareness survey and looking for a connection afterward.

Second, record interview insights, sample context, and experimental questions separately, then connect them with a shared identifier. For environmental or agricultural projects, this makes it possible to trace a research question to the exchange that prompted it and to understand the setting of the sample being discussed.

Third, when teaching or outreach partnerships extend a survey’s reach, record course participation and questionnaire participation separately. Other teams can adapt this collaborative approach while maintaining clear definitions for each set of participation statistics.

Other teams can document feedback using these fields: project question, stakeholder and date, main finding, team discussion, and follow-up direction. Source records can remain within the team, while public pages present thematic summaries with sensitive information removed. This provides a practical way to connect different sources of feedback with project discussions.
